content.text: Spot one half or one quarter in a shape split into equal parts.
Find half of up to 20 things by sharing them into two equal groups.
Find a quarter of up to 20 things by sharing them into four equal groups.

slides.notes:
Running
About 3 minutes. Ask pupils to look carefully at the model and tell a partner what makes the parts halves. Take one or two explanations.

Misconceptions
Pupils may think any two parts make halves, even if the parts are different sizes. Explain that halves must be equal in size.

Background
A shape can be split into equal halves in different ways; the parts do not have to look identical in orientation.

elements.alt: A square is split into two equal parts, with one part shaded.
elements.name: Diagram

content.text: One half is one of two equal parts of a shape.

slides.notes:
Running
About 3 minutes. Ask pupils to explain to a partner how they know the model shows quarters. Invite a pupil to state the definition.

Misconceptions
Pupils may think any four parts make quarters. Emphasise that quarters are four equal parts, not just four parts.

Background
A quarter is one of four equal parts of a whole. Four quarters make one whole.

elements.alt: A circle is split into four equal parts, with one part shaded.
elements.name: Diagram

content.text: One quarter is one of four equal parts of a shape.

slides.notes:
Running
Give pupils about 2 minutes to choose an answer independently, then ask them to explain their choice to a partner. Take a few responses and confirm the answer as a class.

Answers
B: One quarter

Misconceptions
“One whole” means all four parts together, not one part. “One half” is one of two equal parts; with four equal parts, one part is one quarter.

Background
A quarter is one of four equal parts of a whole. The parts must be equal in size, not just four separate regions.

content.text: A rectangle has four equal parts. What is one part?

elements.alt: A circle is split into four equal parts, with one part shaded.
elements.name: Diagram

slides.notes:
Running
About 4 minutes. Model or use counters to share the ten objects into two equal groups. Ask pupils to count each group and state how this gives half.

Misconceptions
Pupils may count all ten counters as the answer, or split them into groups that are not equal. Check that both groups have the same number; five and five make ten.

Background
Sharing equally into two groups is a practical way to find half. The answer is the number in one group, not the total number shared.

elements.alt: Ten counters are shared into two groups of five.
elements.name: Diagram

content.text: Share 10 counters equally into two groups. Each group has 5.

slides.notes:
Running
About 6 minutes. Pupils draw and shade independently, then share 14 counters into two equal groups. Ask them to check the groups match before writing the number in one group.

Answers
1. A rectangle split into two equal parts, with one part shaded.
2. 7

Misconceptions
For the drawing, pupils may shade an unequal part and still call it half; both parts must be equal. For 14, pupils may give 14 or 2 instead of the number in each equal group. Share the counters one at a time between two groups; each group gets 7.

Background
A rectangle can be divided into halves in more than one way, provided the two areas are equal.

content.text: Draw a rectangle. Split it equally and shade one half.
Share 14 counters equally into two groups. Find half.

question.modelAnswer:
1. Two equal parts, one shaded
2. 7 counters

slides.notes:
Running
About 4 minutes. Use counters or the model to share 12 into four equal groups. Have pupils count one group and check that all four groups are equal.

Misconceptions
Pupils may think the answer is 12 because that is the total, or may share unequally. Show that four equal groups of three account for all 12 counters.

Background
Finding a quarter by sharing uses four equal groups; the number in one group is one quarter.

elements.alt: Twelve counters are shared into four groups of three.
elements.name: Diagram

content.text: Share 12 counters equally into four groups. Each group has 3.

slides.notes:
Running
About 5 minutes. Pupils work through both questions, drawing or using counters to make four equal groups. Ask them to explain how they checked their sharing.

Answers
1. 2
2. 1

Misconceptions
Pupils may divide by two rather than by four, giving 4 for the first task or 2 for the second. Remind them that quarters require four equal groups, then count the objects in one group.

Background
These examples use totals that divide exactly into four equal groups: 8 gives groups of 2, and 4 gives groups of 1.

content.text: Share 8 counters equally into four groups. Find one quarter.
Share 4 counters equally into four groups. Find one quarter.

slides.notes:
Running
About 4 minutes. Work through the sharing with counters or the model. Ask pupils to verify the result by counting in fours groups of five, or by adding 5 four times.

Misconceptions
Pupils may answer 20, the total, or give the number of groups rather than the number in one group. Check that four groups of five use all 20 counters.

Background
Repeated sharing into four groups reinforces that one quarter of 20 is found by sharing 20 equally, not by taking away four.

elements.alt: Twenty counters are shared into four groups of five.
elements.name: Diagram

content.text: Share 20 counters equally into four groups. Each group has 5.

slides.notes:
Running
About 3 minutes. Pupils choose an answer independently, then explain how four equal groups help them check it.

Answers
B: 4 counters

Misconceptions
“12 counters” may show that the pupil has taken 4 away from 16 rather than sharing into four equal groups. “8 counters” may show that they have found half instead of a quarter. Explain that four groups of four make 16, so one group contains 4.

Background
This checks whether pupils distinguish quarters from halves and can connect equal sharing to the written answer.

content.text: What is one quarter of 16 counters?

slides.notes:
Running
Allow about 5 minutes. Pupils solve both problems independently, showing how they share the amounts. Then pair them to check their answers and explain how they know the shares are equal.

Answers
1. 9 shells per pot.
2. 8 marbles.

Misconceptions
For the shells, pupils may divide 18 by 3 because they count the two pots and Mia as three sharers. Share between the two pots only: 9 in each. For the marbles, pupils may give 4 because that is a quarter of 16, but the question asks for two bags. Two groups of 4 make 8.

Background
Two quarters make one half. Here, two bags hold half of the 16 marbles: 8.

elements.name: Diagram

content.text: Mia shares 18 shells equally between two pots. How many per pot?
Four bags each hold a quarter of 16 marbles. How many marbles fill two bags?

slides.notes:
Running
About 5 minutes. Pupils complete the exit ticket independently. Collect or check their work to identify who can show equal halves and share amounts into two or four equal groups.

Answers
1. A square split into two equal parts, with one part shaded; for example, a vertical or horizontal split through the middle.
2. 9
3. 4 counters

Misconceptions
For the drawing, pupils may shade unequal parts; halves must be equal. For half of 18, pupils may give 18 or 2 instead of 9; sharing into two equal groups gives 9 in each. For a quarter of 16, pupils may give 8 by finding half or 12 by subtracting 4; four equal groups contain 4 each.

Background
The ticket checks shape halves, finding half by equal sharing, and finding a quarter by equal sharing.

What is one quarter of 16 counters?
